title: Stop Burning Tokens: Why self-improvement needs domain expertise first - Annabell Schäfer, Langfuse

summary: Annabell Schäfer, a Growth Engineer at Langfuse, addresses the problem of token waste in AI agent improvement loops. She frames the current trend where prominent figures advocate designing loops over prompt engineering, but notes they come primarily from a developer perspective. Coding, she argues, set a false precedent because it benefits from an inherently clear target function—whether code compiles. In most other domains (medical compliance, healthcare, chatbots), target functions are far less clear and inherently incomplete, making auto-improvement much harder. She observes that teams investing heavily in target function quality and evaluators are the ones who continuously improve and ship with confidence. She presents a case study: classifying arXiv papers by primary category using title and abstract. This single-label classification task provides a deterministic yes/no target function. The experiment uses a minimal self-optimization loop with GPT-4o-mini as the classifier agent, Claude Opus as the optimizer proposing prompt updates, a GPT-5 prompting guide for context, and a task.md describing the loop. Datasets include 200 fit items, 100 validation items, and 300 test items to prevent overfitting. The loop runs the base prompt, performs error analysis on the fit set, has Opus formulate hypotheses and propose prompt updates, accepts changes only if they improve validation accuracy, and uses stopping criteria of 15 runs or 92% accuracy. Results show a 15% improvement from 68% to 83% accuracy, with the largest single jump—10%—occurring in the first iteration. The system generalized to 80.2% on the unseen test set. The optimizer added classification approaches, rules for distinguishing similar classes, confused pattern guidance, and examples rather than simple label descriptions. Schäfer then addresses how to translate this binary high-signal feedback into other applications. She argues that popular evaluators like correctness, helpfulness, or hallucination are low-signal when placed on numeric scales (0–1, 1–5) because the meaning of each number is rarely defined precisely. Instead, teams should define domain-specific quality criteria as binary checks: Is the answer based on the knowledge base? Is the brand voice correct? Which known failure mode occurred? She stresses working with domain experts to create concrete examples, review sample runs together, and extract implicit knowledge. After deployment, humans must review production data—not just coding agents—to understand shifting failure modes and scope. Finally, she advocates building systems that generalize, using validation mechanisms from traditional ML to prevent overfitting, and giving the loop an escape hatch to stop rather than burn tokens indefinitely. The goal is a collaborative improving system where humans and agents know when to hand off to each other.

sections.title: Introduction and the goal of avoiding token waste
sections.summary: Schäfer introduces herself as a Growth Engineer at Langfuse and frames the talk around stopping token waste by building domain expertise into loop and application design early.

sections.title: The loops trend and coding's false precedent
sections.summary: Discusses the trend of designing loops over prompt engineering (Boris Journey, Peter Steinheimer, Karpathy). Notes these advocates come from a developer perspective where coding has a clear target function: does the code compile. This set a false precedent for other domains.

sections.title: Challenges of target functions in non-coding domains
sections.summary: Explains that in domains like medical compliance, healthcare, and chatbots, target functions are not nearly as clear and are inherently incomplete. Teams investing heavily in target function quality and evaluators are the ones who continuously improve and ship with confidence.

sections.title: Case study: arXiv paper classification experiment
sections.summary: Introduces the clearest-cut target function found: single-label classification of arXiv papers by primary category using title and abstract. The deterministic yes/no (predicted equals true label) allows clear accuracy measurement.

sections.title: Minimal self-optimization loop setup
sections.summary: Details the loop: GPT-4o-mini as the classifier agent with a flat label list prompt, Claude Opus 4.8 as optimizer with GPT-5 prompting guide context, datasets of 200 fit / 100 validate / 300 test items, managed through Langfuse with input and expected output columns.

sections.title: Step-by-step iteration process and stopping criteria
sections.summary: Describes the instructed loop via task markdown: run base prompt for baseline, perform error analysis on fit set looking for error clusters and confused pairs, have Opus propose updates for biggest error category, accept only if validation improves, with stopping criteria of 15 runs or 92% accuracy, then final test set run.

sections.title: Results: 15% improvement and generalization
sections.summary: Reports 15% improvement from 68% to 83% accuracy, with the first iteration jumping 10%. Notes plateau around 80%, generalization to test set at 80.2%. Discovers that authors had creative freedom in choosing labels, introducing ambiguity even in this clear-cut task.

sections.title: Deep dive into the optimizer's reasoning and prompt changes
sections.summary: Examines what the optimizer did: added a general classification approach, rules for distinguishing similar classes, confused pattern guidance, and examples for misclassified pairs rather than label descriptions. The first 10% jump came from identifying 64 errors, dominating patterns, and forming a data-backed hypothesis. Notes that deterministic yes/no target functions barely exist in most real cases.

sections.title: Translating high-signal feedback to other applications
sections.summary: Addresses how to translate binary right/wrong feedback into other domains. Argues that popular scaled evaluators (correctness, helpfulness, hallucination on 0–1 or 1–5 scales) are low-signal because numeric meanings are rarely defined. Recommends domain-specific binary quality criteria instead: is the answer based on the knowledge base, is the brand voice correct, which known failure mode occurred.

sections.title: Working with domain experts and defining what good looks like
sections.summary: Stresses engaging domain experts to create concrete examples, review sample runs together, and extract implicit knowledge about how decisions are made. This helps identify failure modes and define what good means. Notes that data volume plus high-signal feedback form the foundation.

sections.title: Human review of production data and building generalizing systems
sections.summary: Advises reviewing production data as a human, not just with coding agents, to understand shifting failure modes and scope changes. Advocates building systems that generalize using validation mechanisms from traditional ML and giving loops an escape hatch to stop rather than burn tokens indefinitely, enabling human-agent collaboration on an improving system.
